items.content:
Excel is rarely the real problem in Supply Chain Planning.
It is usually the place where the real problem becomes visible.

The system has a number.
The planner knows the number cannot be trusted yet.
The meeting needs a decision.
The business still needs a compromise between service, inventory, cost and capacity.

So the spreadsheet appears.

Not because people love manual work.

Often because the operating model has not answered basic questions.

Who can override the plan?
Which data is trusted enough to act from?
Which exception needs escalation?
Which KPI wins when service and inventory conflict?
Who owns the outcome after the manual adjustment?

If those answers are unclear, a new tool will not remove the spreadsheet.

It will sit next to it.

That is why I do not like the sentence "we need to get rid of Excel."

I would rather ask:
What job is this spreadsheet doing for the organization?

Once you know that, you can decide whether the logic belongs in the system, in the process, in the governance, or in the management rhythm.

Excel is not always the enemy.
Sometimes it is the evidence.

Which spreadsheet in your organization would be dangerous to delete tomorrow?

The recommendation looks useful.

Then Monday arrives.

The planner returns to the spreadsheet.
The manager reviews the same report.

The pilot proved that the technology works.

For me, adoption starts when work changes.
Someone makes a decision differently.
A manual step disappears.
The management review becomes sharper.
An exception reaches the right owner without another escalation.

That is the gap between a successful demo and operational value.

What must change on Monday morning before you call an AI pilot successful?

items.content:
AI will not fix a weak supply chain.
It will expose it faster.

That is uncomfortable, but useful.
When a planning process has no clear owner, AI does not create ownership. It produces faster recommendations that nobody feels accountable to accept.
When master data is unreliable, AI does not create trust. It makes the data problem visible in every exception.
When demand, supply, inventory and capacity are managed in separate conversations, AI does not connect the business. It gives each function a better reason to defend its own view.
This is why many companies start in the wrong place.

They ask:
What AI tool should we test?

The better question is:
Which planning decision should become faster, cheaper or more reliable?

That question changes the discussion.
It forces a leader to define the owner.
It forces the team to name the input data.
It forces finance and operations to agree on the KPI tradeoff.
It forces IT to support a real process, not a slide.
AI can improve Supply Chain Planning. I believe that strongly.
However, it rewards companies that already know how decisions should work.
If the operating model is unclear, AI becomes another layer on top of unclear work.

The practical starting point is simple:
Pick one planning decision and trace it from trigger to owner to KPI to escalation.
If that path is unclear, fix that before adding an agent.

Where does accountability disappear first in your planning process?

Why was the expedite approved?

Why was capacity moved?

Decisions teach AI how the business thinks.

If you only capture the data, the system sees the result.

If you also capture the decision, the constraint and the reasoning, the system starts to see the operating logic.

This is where many AI projects in Supply Chain get stuck.

They try to automate the visible part.

But the real decision logic is still hidden in meetings, emails and peopleâ€™s heads.

That is not less ambitious.

items.content:
The best executor on my team had the hardest time becoming a project owner.

Everything was delivered I asked. Precisely. On time. Zero surprises. That was the problem.

When I stopped giving detailed instructions and said "this is your domain, define the path," he froze. Not because he was not capable. Because his entire career rewarded following instructions, not creating them.

The shift from "what do you need me to do" to "here is what I think we should do" does not happen overnight. And it starts with the director tolerating silence instead of filling it with directions.

Here is what I learned. When someone asks me "what should I do," my instinct is to answer. That would solve today's problem. It would also guarantee that the same person comes back next week with the same question.

So I push back. Not harshly. "What have you considered so far? What are the options?"

I know how this feels from the other side. When your boss answers your question with a question, it can feel like a test. It is not. It is the only way I have found to build leaders who think for themselves instead of waiting for approval.

The discomfort is real. For both sides. That is the signal that something is changing.

After 30 days of deployment, you face one decision: scale, fix, or stop.

Most organizations skip this step. They assume deployment equals adoption.

Before you decide, run three checks.

Look for parallel processes. Who is running the old process alongside the new one "just to verify"? That person is not verifying. They are protecting themselves.

Watch what managers actually do. Not what they say in meetings. If the manager still asks for the old report format, the team reads that as a signal.

Check the corridor narrative. What do people say about the tool when you are not in the room? That is the truth about your adoption.

If adoption grows: scale to the next team.
If adoption is flat: fix the block before expanding.
If adoption declines: stop. Something fundamental is broken.

A project leader would move on at this point. A product leader stays and makes the call. That distinction decides whether the tool lives or dies.

The return on empowering your team is not measured in the first quarter.

Right now, my team moves slower than if I dictated every step. Some decisions take longer. Some paths turn out wrong. That is the cost.

Every director reading this has the same question: how do you sell this to your own boss?

I do not hide it. I explain that we are building leadership capacity alongside technical capability. The first quarter shows slower delivery. By the second quarter, five people run initiatives independently instead of one person running five things through proxies.

Most senior leaders understand that math when you frame it as scalability, not experimentation.

The return: five people who assess risk before it arrives. Who propose solutions instead of waiting for approvals. Who own outcomes, not tasks. Plus one director who stays sharp by running his own project alongside the team.

A team that thinks for itself generates capacity that one manager thinking for five never could.

And if you are on the other side of this. If you just got handed a project and more freedom than you expected. Start with the smallest useful action. Test one thing. Report what happened. Ask for feedback on your approach, not for instructions on what to do next.

That shift is the moment when ownership becomes real.

AI-Ready Process Checklist

Before you automate a Supply Chain process with AI, check if the process is actually ready.

Not technically ready.

Operationally ready.

Ask seven questions:

1. What decision repeats often enough to matter?
2. What data is used to make it?
3. Who owns the outcome when the decision is wrong?
4. Which constraints must never be violated?
5. What human knowledge is used but not written anywhere?
6. When should the AI act and when should it ask for review?
7. How will we know after 30 or 60 days that the process improved?

If you cannot answer these questions, the issue is probably not the AI tool.

The issue is that the process is not yet legible enough to automate.

That is not a failure.

It is the work.

Make the process visible first.

Then automate one decision flow.

Then redesign the next one.

This is how AI transformation becomes real.

Not by jumping from today’s process to full orchestration.

By rebuilding the process decision by decision.

Four weeks. Four articles. One operating question: why do AI tools that work perfectly get used by almost nobody?

Here is what I covered:

Week 11: the personal layer. Leaders who approve AI budgets but never build a real habit with the tool. If the top does not use it, the organization will not either.

Week 12: the structural layer. Projects that end at go-live. No clear owner for what comes after. The fix: one person accountable from delivery through adoption.

Week 13: the behavioral layer. The spreadsheet comfort zone. The missing permission. The busyness trap. Three patterns that quietly kill adoption.

Week 14: the playbook. What to do in the first 30 days. Week by week. Permission signal. Spreadsheet partner. Snowball effect. Honest checkpoint.

None of these layers works alone. The personal, structural, and behavioral pieces together create the conditions where a good AI tool becomes how people actually work.

If you are running an AI initiative and adoption is not where you expected, start with one question: which layer is missing?

First reflection after Gartner Supply Chain Symposium in Barcelona.

Six months ago, I questioned how useful consulting firms would remain in the age of AI.

After three days, my view is more precise.

For me personally, consulting is less needed than before.

For many businesses, it may be needed more than ever.

But only if the role changes.

Gartner has a strong opportunity here. The focus on AI was clear, practical and much broader than I expected. Not only in Supply Chain, but across almost every business function.

What I also liked was the growing honesty about AI risk.

There is still a big gap between three things.

What leaders think AI will do.

What software companies say their tools can do.

What actually gets delivered in daily operations.

The direction is clear. AI will change Supply Chain.

But we cannot simply add AI on top of old processes and expect a different outcome.

One analogy stayed with me.

Electricity did not truly transform factories when it was first introduced. The real change came later, when factories were redesigned around electricity.

AI may follow the same path.

The real work is not only implementing AI tools.

The real work is redesigning processes around AI driven decisions.

15 minutes. That is how much time the AI tool saved on day one.

The team called it "not worth the learning curve."

Two months later, that same team was saving four hours per planner per week. They stopped calling it worthless somewhere around week three.

The problem is not the tool. It is the expectation. Teams expect total change on day one. They want the full replacement of their process. When they get 15 minutes back instead, they give up.

The teams that succeed understand the snowball effect.

You start with one task. 15 minutes saved. You invest those 15 minutes into learning the next use case. That saves another 15. Over weeks, the compound effect is significant.

But you have to reset the narrative. Not "this tool will change how you work." Instead: "this tool will give you back 15 minutes tomorrow."

The snowball starts small. It always does.

items.content:
The hardest part of AI adoption is not convincing people that AI works.

It is helping them accept that the current process does not.

I have seen this pattern many times in large operations.

The first discussion is usually about the tool.
* Which model?
* Which platform?
* Which data source?

But after a few hours, the real questions appear.

* Who can override the recommendation?
* Who owns the exception?
* Which KPI wins when service and inventory conflict?
* Who explains the tradeoff to finance?
* Who decides when the plan is good enough?

This is where AI becomes useful.

Not because it answers everything.

Because it makes weak decisions harder to hide.

For many teams, that is uncomfortable.

A spreadsheet can absorb unclear ownership for years.

An AI agent cannot.

It needs a decision path.

If the path does not exist, the project slows down.

The lesson is clear for me.

Before asking whether your supply chain is ready for AI, ask whether your planning process is ready to be questioned.

That is usually the better test.

items.content:
"I am here when you need me" sounds like soft leadership. It is the hardest thing I do.

When a leader on my team hesitates, every instinct says step in. Fix it. Give the answer. That would solve today's problem and guarantee tomorrow's dependency.

The alternative: wait. Let them struggle. Answer when asked. Do not volunteer the solution before they have tried to find it themselves.

There is a specific moment when this works. A leader comes to me and says "I am stuck, here is what I have tried, what do you think." That is a productive conversation. They have done the thinking. They have a position. I can challenge or confirm it. Either way, they leave with a decision they own.

Compare that to "What should I do?" That conversation produces instructions, not ownership.

The cost is real. Sometimes my leaders take a direction I would not have chosen. Sometimes a week goes into an approach I knew would not work. I watch it happen.

But a leader who found the right approach on their own will defend it with conviction. Will troubleshoot it when problems appear. Will improve it without being asked. Because it is theirs.

That is worth more than three weeks of saved time.

One AI project improves one process. Six connected AI projects change how a division operates.

Each leader on my team owns a separate AI initiative. Different domains. Different tools. Different user groups. On the surface, six separate projects.

In practice, they feed each other. When the data quality project delivers clean inputs, the planning project runs better. When planning produces reliable forecasts, operations makes sharper decisions. When operations automates routine checks, it frees time for capacity analysis.

This only works if each leader understands not just their own piece, but how it connects to the others.

That is why my team talks to each other about their projects. Not because I scheduled a sync meeting. Because they figured out their outcomes depend on each other. The planning lead needs to know what the data quality lead is building. The operations lead needs to understand how planning outputs will change.

These conversations happen because the structure creates natural dependencies. Not because I drew a RACI matrix.

Autonomy without collaboration produces six isolated tools. Autonomy with collaboration produces one integrated capability.

Are your AI projects connected, or running in parallel silos?

items.content:
I talk to Supply Chain Directors regularly.

One pattern keeps showing up. 
The gap between what they expected from Agentic AI and what actually happened after go-live.

Here's what surprises them most.

1. It works best on repetitive decisions, not strategic ones. 
The biggest wins came from high-volume, rule-based calls. Expedite or not. Allocate or hold. Not from strategy. 
The system handles the noise. People handle the judgment calls.

2. Deployment takes 6–9 months, not 6 weeks.
Vendors promise fast. Reality is slow. 
Change management, data cleanup, process redesign. 
None of that fits in a sprint.

3. The biggest win isn't the outcome. It's decision transparency.
Planners stopped asking "why did the system do that?" They started understanding it. 
Teams work differently once that shift happens.

4. Clean data isn't optional.
Put an agent on top of messy data and you get wrong answers delivered with confidence. 
The AI doesn't know it's wrong. That's the risk.
5. People don't lose their jobs. Their jobs change.
The repetitive part gets automated. 
The judgment part gets more visible, and more accountable.

These are patterns, not laws. I could be wrong on some of them.

Which one matches your reality?

I gave my team full ownership of six AI projects. Some of them struggled with it.

Not because the projects were too hard. Because the freedom was too much.

When you tell experienced leaders "this is your domain, define the path yourself," two things happen. Some move immediately. They explore, test, start building. Others freeze. They ask for detailed instructions. They want examples of what the output should look like. They wait.

That second reaction is not a weakness. It is a product of decades in organizations that rewarded following instructions and punished independent decisions that went wrong.

This week's article is about what happens next. How to hold the line between support and micromanagement. Why I kept one project for myself to stay honest about what I am asking of them. And what it costs in the short term to build a team that thinks for itself.

This is not leadership theory. This is what I am going through right now, across six AI initiatives in a large supply chain organization.

Full article in the newsletter.

Here's the DM system that turns them into clients:

1. Generate leads

→ Inbound DMs from people who like your post
→ Outbound to warm leads already engaging with you

2. Pre-qualify your leads 

✅ Not every lead deserves your energy

→ Qualify the lead in the DMs before a call
→ Do they fit your ideal client profile?
→ Can they actually afford to buy?
→ Is this the right moment for them?

3. Build the relationship

✅ Never pitch on the first message

→ "What’s your goal for the rest of the year?"
→ Show genuine interest before you show your offer
→ People buy from people they trust, not people who sell at them

4. Identify the need 

✅ You need context before you pitch anything

→ "Walk me through where you're at right now."
→ What have they already tried?
→ What's working?
→ What isn't? 

5. Find out where they want to be

✅ Identify exactly where they want to go 

→ "What does success look like for you in six months?"
→ The gap between now and desired outcome is where your offer lives
→ Identify the gap and it will help you sell

6. Dig into what's stopping them

✅ What is stopping them get from X to Y

→ "What's the biggest thing holding you back?"
→ Listen more than you talk here
→ The blocker is usually where your offer fits perfectly

7. Gauge urgency

✅ How long have they been sitting with this problem?

→ Long-standing pain = high priority = ready to invest
→ Recent pain = still exploring = not ready yet
→ Urgency tells you everything about timing

8. Give them a clear next step

✅ If they tick every box move decisively.

→ Send your offer details or suggest a call
→ Never leave a conversation without a defined action
→ If they say no, find out why
→ Every lost deal is a learning
